description: How ice sheet growth and melting drive global sea level change, with drowned forest evidence.
content_html:
Why Does the Sea Rise and Fall?

Sea level is not fixed. Over geological time, it has risen and fallen by hundreds of metres — and those changes have left striking evidence in the geological record. The primary control on global sea level is how much water is stored as ice. When continental ice sheets grow, they lock up vast amounts of water as solid ice, and sea levels around the world fall. When those ice sheets melt, the water returns to the oceans and sea levels rise. This is eustatic sea level change — a global shift driven by changes in ocean water volume.

Understanding the link between ice and sea level is central to this unit. It connects the icehouse and greenhouse climate states you studied in the previous lesson directly to the landscape evidence we can see on coastlines and on the seabed today. Examiners regularly ask students to explain the mechanism behind sea level change, so mastering the cause-and-effect chain is essential.

Key Fact

During an icehouse period, continental ice sheets grow by accumulating snow and ice. This locks water away from the ocean, reducing its volume. Global sea levels therefore fall — by as much as 120 metres during the peak of the last glaciation about 20,000 years ago. During warming, ice sheets melt and return water to the ocean, causing sea levels to rise.

Drowned Forests: Evidence for Rising Seas

Drowned forests are one of the most dramatic pieces of evidence for post-glacial sea level rise. Around the coasts of Britain — at places such as Borth in Wales, Redcar in Yorkshire and various beaches in Cornwall — ancient tree stumps are exposed at low tide. These are the remains of forests that grew on dry land thousands of years ago, during and after the last glaciation when sea levels were much lower than today.

As the ice sheets of the last glaciation melted (beginning around 18,000 years ago), meltwater flooded back into the ocean and sea levels rose rapidly. The forests that had colonised low-lying coastal land were progressively submerged. Peat layers associated with the tree roots are often preserved beneath beach sediment, and radiocarbon dating of this peat confirms ages of roughly 4,000–8,000 years for many British drowned forests — showing that significant sea level rise occurred in the early Holocene after the main ice retreat.

During the peak of the last glaciation, sea levels were roughly 120 metres lower than today and a large area of dry land connected Britain to mainland Europe across what is now the southern North Sea. Geologists call this area Doggerland. It was a landscape of rivers, lakes and forests, inhabited by early humans. As the Pleistocene ice sheets melted during the Holocene, sea levels rose and Doggerland was progressively flooded. By about 6,500 years ago, Britain had become an island. Trawler nets in the North Sea occasionally dredge up worked flint tools and animal bones, confirming the former existence of this inhabited landscape beneath the sea.

The Scale of Ice: How Much Sea Level Change?

The size of an ice sheet determines how much sea level falls when it forms. The larger the ice extent, the more water is removed from the oceans. During the Last Glacial Maximum around 20,000 years ago, ice sheets covered much of North America, Scandinavia, and Britain north of the Thames–Severn line. Global sea levels were approximately 120 metres below their current level. Conversely, if the current Antarctic ice sheet were to melt completely, sea levels would rise by approximately 58 metres — enough to flood all coastal cities on Earth.

Key Fact

At the peak of the last glaciation (approximately 20,000 years ago), global sea levels were about 120 metres lower than present. This was enough to expose a land bridge between Britain and Europe (Doggerland) and to leave drowned forests along Britain’s current coastline as evidence of the lower sea level.

Global Warming, Global Cooling, and Ice Extent

The chain of causation runs in both directions. Global warming reduces ice extent by increasing melt rates. Reduced ice extent means less water stored as ice, so sea levels rise. Global cooling has the opposite effect: more snow falls than melts, ice sheets grow, water is removed from the oceans, and sea levels fall.

This process operates on a range of timescales. Orbital cycles (changes in the shape of Earth’s orbit and the tilt of its axis) drive glacial–interglacial cycles over periods of 20,000–100,000 years. Over millions of years, atmospheric carbon dioxide levels — influenced by volcanic activity and the weathering of rocks — are the dominant control on global temperature and therefore on ice volume and sea level. Both mechanisms are explored in the following lessons.

Eustatic sea level change is a global process, but local sea level change is also influenced by isostasy. When a thick ice sheet sits on a continent, its weight depresses the crust downward. When the ice melts, the crust slowly rebounds upward — a process called post-glacial isostatic rebound. In Scotland, the crust is still rising by about 1–2 mm per year because of the unloading of Pleistocene ice. This means local relative sea level in Scotland is falling even as global eustatic sea level rises. Southern England, further from the centre of ice loading, is slowly tilting downward into the North Sea. Isostasy and eustasy act simultaneously and must be distinguished in exam answers about sea level change.

Reading Sea Level Change from the Rock Record

Past sea level changes are also recorded in sedimentary sequences. When sea level rises, marine sediments (muds, sands, limestones) are deposited over formerly terrestrial or coastal deposits. When sea level falls, erosion may occur and a gap in the record — an unconformity — can result. Sequences of alternating marine and terrestrial sediments indicate repeated sea level rises and falls, and are common throughout the British Palaeozoic and Mesozoic rock record.
exam_tip_html: When asked to explain sea level change, always give the full mechanism: state whether ice is growing or melting, explain what happens to water volume in the ocean as a result, and then state the direction of sea level change. One-step answers (“sea level rose because it got warmer”) will only earn one mark. For questions involving drowned forests or Doggerland, link the evidence explicitly to post-glacial sea level rise — name the process (ice sheet melting), the direction of change (sea level rise), and explain why dry land became submerged. Watch out for questions that ask you to distinguish eustatic sea level change from isostatic (land level) change — these are tested separately.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Global sea level is controlled by ice volume: growing ice sheets lock water away from the ocean, lowering sea level; melting ice sheets return water to the ocean, raising sea level. At the Last Glacial Maximum, sea levels were about 120 metres below present.
  • Drowned forests (such as those at Borth, Wales, and Redcar, Yorkshire) are exposed at low tide and provide evidence for post-glacial sea level rise as Pleistocene ice sheets melted and submerged formerly dry coastal land.
  • Eustatic (global ocean volume) changes must be distinguished from isostatic (crustal rebound) effects: Scotland is still rising as a result of post-glacial isostatic rebound, while southern England is slowly subsiding.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes the cause of eustatic sea level fall?
A) The crust subsides under the weight of ice
B) More water evaporates from the ocean surface
C) Continental ice sheets grow, locking water away from the ocean
D) Ocean basins become deeper as tectonic plates move apart
practice_questions.marks: C) Continental ice sheets grow, locking water away from the ocean [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name one location in Britain where a drowned forest can be observed at low tide.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any correct location, e.g. Borth (Wales) / Redcar (Yorkshire) / Cornwall coastal beaches [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe how the growth of a continental ice sheet leads to a fall in global sea level.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying that water is removed from the ocean and stored as ice / precipitation falls as snow and accumulates. One mark for stating that this reduces the volume of water in the ocean, causing sea level to fall. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: A drowned forest is found exposed on a beach at low tide. Explain what this tells geologists about past sea levels and how those sea levels changed.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that trees grew on dry land when sea levels were lower than today (during the Pleistocene glaciation, when ice sheets stored large amounts of water); as the ice sheets melted at the end of the last glaciation, meltwater returned to the ocean, sea level rose progressively, and the former land surface was submerged; the preserved tree stumps now sit below the current high tide mark, proving that sea level was lower when the forest was alive.
Secure: Identifies lower past sea level (glaciation) and subsequent sea level rise (melting); two of three points developed.
Developing: States that sea level used to be lower and that the land was flooded, without linking to ice sheet changes.
Emerging: States that there used to be a forest here without explaining sea level change. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between eustatic sea level change and isostatic sea level change, using Scotland as an example of isostatic change.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Defines eustatic as a global change in ocean water volume (driven by ice growth/melting); defines isostatic as a local change in land height relative to the sea (driven by crustal loading/unloading); applies isostasy to Scotland — the crust was depressed by Pleistocene ice and is now slowly rebounding upward as the ice is gone, so Scotland’s land surface is rising and local relative sea level is falling even as global eustatic sea level rises.
Secure: Correctly defines both terms and applies one to Scotland; all three elements present but explanation less full.
Developing: Defines one term correctly; partial application to Scotland.
Emerging: Confuses the two terms or gives only one correct point. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate how well drowned forests and other coastal evidence can be used to reconstruct past sea level changes. In your answer, discuss both the strengths and limitations of this type of evidence.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Strengths — drowned forests provide direct physical evidence (tree stumps, peat, radiocarbon-dateable organic material) of past land surfaces below sea level, allowing relative sea level to be quantified and dated; Doggerland evidence (flint tools from trawlers) confirms human habitation of now-submerged land. Limitations — evidence is fragmentary (wave action destroys many sites); isostatic vs eustatic contributions cannot always be separated from coastal evidence alone; relative sea level curves may differ between regions because of differential isostatic rebound; dating uncertainty. Reaches a reasoned conclusion about the value and limitations of coastal evidence.
Secure: Covers at least two strengths and one limitation with specific examples; conclusion present.
Developing: Describes drowned forests as evidence without evaluating strengths/limitations in depth.
Emerging: Simple points about sea level change without engaging with the question of how useful the evidence is. [6 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: What happens to global sea level when continental ice sheets grow?
options: It falls, because water is locked in ice
It rises, because glaciers push water into the ocean

knowledge_checks.q: By approximately how many metres was sea level lower than today at the Last Glacial Maximum (~20,000 years ago)?
Drowned forests are exposed at low tide because sea levels have _____ since the forests were alive, submerging the former land surface.
Eustatic sea level change is driven by changes in the _____ of water in the ocean.
Match each term to its correct description:
right: Global change in sea level due to changing ocean water volume
Slow upward movement of the crust after ice sheet removal
Ancient tree stumps submerged by rising post-glacial seas

flashcard_questions.q: What is eustatic sea level change?
flashcard_questions.a: A worldwide change in sea level caused by a change in ocean water volume, not by land movement.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does sea level fall when continental ice sheets grow?
flashcard_questions.a: Water is removed from the ocean and stored as ice, reducing the ocean's total volume.

flashcard_questions.q: By approximately how much did global sea level fall at the Last Glacial Maximum?
flashcard_questions.a: About 120 metres below present sea level.

flashcard_questions.q: What are drowned forests and what do they prove about past sea levels?
flashcard_questions.a: Ancient submerged tree stumps proving the land was once above sea level when seas were lower.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one location in Britain where a drowned forest is exposed at low tide.
What was Doggerland and why does it no longer exist?
flashcard_questions.a: A dry land area connecting Britain to Europe, flooded by rising post-glacial seas about 6,500 years ago.
The slow upward rise of the crust after the weight of an ice sheet is removed by melting.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is Scotland's land surface still rising today?
flashcard_questions.a: Post-glacial isostatic rebound — the crust is still recovering from being depressed by Pleistocene ice.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between eustatic and isostatic sea level change?
flashcard_questions.a: Eustatic is global (ocean volume); isostatic is local (land height relative to sea).

flashcard_questions.q: What does an unconformity in a sedimentary sequence often indicate?
flashcard_questions.a: A period of erosion or non-deposition, often linked to a sea level fall exposing the surface.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens to sea level when global warming causes ice sheets to melt?
flashcard_questions.a: Sea level rises, because meltwater returns to the ocean, increasing its volume.

glossary_terms.definition: Large masses of ice covering a substantial area of a continent, formed by the accumulation and compaction of snow over thousands of years.
A worldwide change in sea level caused by a change in the volume of water in the oceans, as opposed to local land movements.
Ancient tree stumps and root systems preserved on an intertidal beach or sea floor, exposed at low tide, showing that the area was once dry land above sea level.
A sustained increase in average global surface temperature, causing ice to melt and sea level to rise.
A sustained decrease in average global surface temperature, causing ice sheets to grow and sea level to fall.
The adjustment of the Earth's crust in response to changes in the weight placed upon it, such as the loading and unloading of ice sheets.
A surface of erosion or non-deposition that separates younger strata from older strata, representing a gap in the geological record.
